```{r}
# Load the required packages
library(tidyverse)
library(here)

# Import the dataset
heart <- read.csv(
  "C:/Users/nafis/OneDrive/Documents/Data_Mining_Modeling_Biostat/Practice_Problem_01/healthcare-dataset-stroke-data.csv",
  header = TRUE,
  stringsAsFactors = TRUE
)

# Examine the two variables
heart %>%
  select(bmi, avg_glucose_level) %>%
  head()
```

> "BMI is the independent variable because it is being used to predict average glucose level, which is the dependent variable. BMI is easier to clinically evaluate because it only requires a patient's height and weight, whereas measuring blood glucose requires a blood sample or specialized glucose-monitoring equipment."

```{r}
# Check the structure and missing values
str(heart)
summary(heart)

# Data wrangling
heart_clean <- heart %>%
  select(bmi, avg_glucose_level) %>%
  mutate(bmi = as.numeric(as.character(bmi))) %>%
  drop_na(bmi, avg_glucose_level)

# Check the cleaned dataset
str(heart_clean)
nrow(heart_clean)

# Run a linear regression model
glucose_model <- lm(avg_glucose_level ~ bmi, data = heart_clean)

# View the results
summary(glucose_model)
```

> "Before running the linear regression model, the BMI and average glucose level columns were selected. BMI was converted into a numeric variable, and observations containing missing values were removed, leaving 4,909 observations. A linear regression model was performed using BMI as the independent variable and average glucose level as the dependent variable. The results showed a statistically significant positive relationship between BMI and average glucose level (p < 0.05). However, the R-squared value of 0.0308 indicates that BMI explains only approximately 3.08% of the variation in average glucose levels. Therefore, although BMI is a statistically significant predictor of average glucose level, the relationship is relatively weak."

```{r}
# Calculate the slope
slope <- sum(
  (heart_clean$bmi - mean(heart_clean$bmi)) *
  (heart_clean$avg_glucose_level - mean(heart_clean$avg_glucose_level))
) / sum(
  (heart_clean$bmi - mean(heart_clean$bmi))^2
)

# Calculate the intercept
intercept <- mean(heart_clean$avg_glucose_level) -
  slope * mean(heart_clean$bmi)

# Create a function to predict glucose level from BMI
predict_glucose <- function(bmi) {
  predicted_glucose <- intercept + slope * bmi
  return(predicted_glucose)
}

# Test the function using a BMI of 25
predict_glucose(25)

# Test the function using a BMI of 30
predict_glucose(30)
```

> "A function called predict_glucose was created using the slope and intercept of the linear regression equation to predict average glucose level from BMI. The function estimates an average glucose level of 101.44 for a patient with a BMI of 25 and 106.40 for a patient with a BMI of 30. The positive slope indicates that predicted average glucose level increases by approximately 0.99 units for every one-unit increase in BMI. However, because the correlation is weak, BMI alone is not a strong predictor of glucose level."
